operator_io_quirks: All identifiers are backtick-quoted in DDL; tables are mixed-case (Addresses, Department_Store_Chain, Staff_Department_Assignments) - generated SQL must double-quote with original case.
Tiny DB: every table <=15 rows, so read_schema's 300k cap never triggers; original_values are complete.

DATETIME columns store TEXT 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS' (space separator, no T, no fractional seconds); declared type DATETIME dispatches to Date fuzzer (not Number) because first element is not int-parsable.
DECIMAL(19,4) columns (product_price, total_value_purchased) store REAL storage class; Number fuzzer with scale=19, precision=4 -> huge range [-1e19,1e19].
total_amount_purchased is VARCHAR(80) but stores numeric-looking text ('89366.05'); String fuzzer will treat as int-like and add +-1 variants.
store_name has distinct=1 with the literal value 'store_name' (placeholder junk in original) - String fuzzer will sample it as an element.

Composite PKs: Supplier_Addresses(supplier_id,address_id), Customer_Addresses(customer_id,address_id), Product_Suppliers(product_id,supplier_id), Staff_Department_Assignments(staff_id,department_id) - composite-PK members get max_l0=30 cap.
All FKs point to existing parents with unique PKs; no dangling FKs, no self-references, no non-unique parents.

NOT NULL columns: payment_method_code, product_type_code, order_status_code, job_title_code, all date_from/date_supplied_from/date_assigned_from, all FK child cols in junction tables - TS does not enforce NOT NULL in Python, so insert failures will drop rows.
staff_gender VARCHAR(1) stores '0'/'1' (int-like strings) - String fuzzer will add str(i+1)/str(i-1) variants.
customer_code VARCHAR(20) stores 3-digit strings ('401','665') - int-like, String fuzzer perturbs to +-1.
No views, triggers, or indexes beyond PKs in DDL; empty clone is cheap.
operator_ts_expectations: Date fuzzer with template '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' (first parsable element) for all DATETIME columns; range = [min,max] of parsed elements, so fresh dates cluster in 2014-2018 window - misses on queries filtering outside that window (FN).
Number fuzzer for INTEGER PKs: range [-10^0,10^0]=[-1,1] with scale=0, so PKs are tiny ints {-1,0,1} perturbed - implausible vs original 1..15, drives FN on 'id > 5' style filters.
Number fuzzer for DECIMAL(19,4): scale=19 -> range [-1e19,1e19], wildly implausible prices - FN on price range predicates.
String fuzzer for VARCHAR(80) names/emails/phones: random CHARSET strings with contamination, plus 5 original samples - loses email/phone format structure, FN on LIKE '%@%' or regex-style predicates.

String fuzzer for low-cardinality enums (payment_method_code, product_type_code, order_status_code, job_title_code, staff_gender, dept_store_chain_name): samples from 2-5 originals + random strings, so enum equality predicates often miss (FN) and random strings create implausible values (FP on 'not in enum' predicates).

FK columns draw from parent's FINAL filtered values with replacement - junction tables get duplicate (child,parent) pairs before PK dedup, then sample_fresh_primary_keys keeps first occurrence, shrinking junction tables below requested size.

Composite PK dedup on junction tables: with small parent sizes (Suppliers=4, Addresses=15), Product_Suppliers/Supplier_Addresses collapse to at most 4*15=60 distinct pairs but requested size may be 30-2500, so many rows dropped.
store_name distinct=1 ('store_name' literal) means String fuzzer's element pool is degenerate - fresh draws dominate, losing the placeholder value.
No NOT NULL enforcement: rows with NULL in payment_method_code etc. fail insert and are silently skipped, so Customers/Products/Customer_Orders may end up smaller than requested.
Date fuzzer p-inversion: p=0.2 means element returned w.p. 0.2, fresh date w.p. 0.8 - fresh dates dominate, so date-range queries see mostly synthetic dates.
Missing ties/duplicates: original has distinct=rows for most columns (no ties), so TS-generated instances with duplicate values may cause FP on GROUP BY / DISTINCT predicates that assume uniqueness.
